title.text: Functions, notation and logarithms: why AI adds log-probabilities

objects.text: A language model gives every possible next word a probability. Why does training work with the logarithm of that probability?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 1 of 18  |  Foundations
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning. I am Jotham, and I will teach you the mathematics under modern AI, with a picture first, then a calculation by hand, then the same idea on a computer, and then where it appears in real AI tools. Today is the first step.

We learn the notation, and we meet the logarithm. By the end you will understand why training a language model uses the logarithm of a probability.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Read sigma notation and function notation, and evaluate both by hand
Use exponentials and logarithms, and the three log rules, to turn a product into a sum
Compute the log-probability of a word and of a sentence in Python and in a spreadsheet

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can read sigma notation and function notation and work them out by hand. You can use exponentials and logarithms, with the three log rules, to turn a product into a sum. And you can compute the log-probability of a word and of a whole sentence, in Python or in a spreadsheet, with the same answers in both.

We build up to one real question from AI, and you will be able to answer it before we leave.

title.text:
Your two hours: sums, functions
and logarithms, then the lab, then AI

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas first. Then the lab, in Python or in a spreadsheet. Then where it shows up in AI.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes are this welcome. Then thirty-five minutes of ideas with pictures, a break, and a forty-five minute lab where you work in Python or in a spreadsheet on the same numbers. The last twenty minutes show where today appears in AI tools, with an exit check, and then you save your work.

The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The symbol Σ means add up. Sigma notation is a short way to write a long sum.
A rule that turns each input number into one output number, written f(x).
A function where the input is a power, such as 2ˣ (2 to the power x). It grows by repeated multiplying.
The inverse of an exponential. The natural logarithm ln uses the base e ≈ 2.71828.
The natural logarithm of a probability. It is zero or negative, because a probability is at most 1.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Sigma notation. The symbol Σ means add up. Sigma notation is a short way to write a long sum.

Function. A rule that turns each input number into one output number, written f(x).

Exponential function. A function where the input is a power, such as 2ˣ (2 to the power x). It grows by repeated multiplying.

Logarithm (ln). The inverse of an exponential. The natural logarithm ln uses the base e ≈ 2.71828.

Log-probability. The natural logarithm of a probability. It is zero or negative, because a probability is at most 1.

title.text:
The sigma symbol is a short
way to write a long sum

objects.alt: The sigma symbol is a short way to write a long sum

objects.text: Sigma notation: the capital Greek letter Σ means add up.

runs.text: Below Σ, i = 1 is where to start. Above Σ, the 4 is where to stop.
Each box is one value, x with its index i.
The values 3, 5, 2 and 8 add up to 18.

slides.notes:
This is sigma notation. The big symbol is the Greek capital letter sigma, and it means add up. Underneath it, i equals one tells you where to start counting. On top, the four tells you where to stop. Then x with a little i is the value at position i.

So this expression says add the first, second, third and fourth values. Here that is three plus five plus two plus eight, which is eighteen. The small letter i is called the index, and it counts the position in the list. Try writing the sum of the first three values yourself: it comes to ten.

title.text:
Sigma notation in action: the five
next-word probabilities add up to 1

objects.alt: Sigma notation in action: the five next-word probabilities add up to 1

rows.text: The index: the position in the list (1, 2, 3 ...).
The probability of word i after "The capital of Uganda is".

objects.text: Illustrative (made-up numbers): Kampala 0.62, Entebbe 0.18, a 0.10, the 0.06, Nairobi 0.04.

slides.notes:
The same idea now meets the numbers we use all day. A language model has to guess the next word after the capital of Uganda is. It gives five candidate words a probability each. A probability is a number from zero to one, where one means certain. These numbers are made up to show the arithmetic.

The sigma sum adds them: zero point six two, plus zero point one eight, plus zero point one, plus zero point zero six, plus zero point zero four. The total is exactly one, because the model must choose something. A total of two would be a mistake: the model would be more than certain, which makes no sense.

title.text:
A function turns each input number
into exactly one output number

objects.alt: A function turns each input number into exactly one output number

objects.text: A function is a rule. Give it an input x and it returns one output, written f(x).

runs.text: Here the rule is f(x) = 2x + 1: double the input, then add 1.
Put in x = 3. Double it to get 6, add 1, and f(3) = 7.
The same input always gives the same output.

slides.notes:
A function is a rule with one job. You give it an input, called x, and it gives back exactly one output, which we write f of x. In this picture the rule is two x plus one. So double the input and add one. If x is three, double it to get six, add one, and f of three is seven.

The machine in the middle is the rule. The important property is that the same input always gives the same output, every time you ask. What does f of ten give?

title.text:
A graph draws every input
and its output as a point

objects.alt: A graph draws every input and its output as a point

objects.text: A graph plots each pair (x, f(x)) as a point. Joining the points draws the curve.

runs.text: Across: the inputs x. Up: the outputs f(x).
Each gold dot is one pair, such as x = 3 and f(3) = 7.
Each step of 1 in x adds 2: a straight line.

slides.notes:
A graph is a picture of a function. The horizontal axis holds the inputs and the vertical axis holds the outputs. Each gold dot is one pair, an input and the output the rule gave. At x equals three the output is seven, so there is a dot at three across and seven up.

Join all the dots and you get the curve of the function. For this rule the curve is a straight line, because every step of one in x adds two to the output. That number two is the slope. With the rule three x plus one, the slope would be three.

title.text:
The function f(x) = wx + b is the
building block of machine learning

objects.alt: The function f(x) = wx + b is the building block of machine learning

rows.text: The output for the input x.
The weight: how much the output grows when x grows by 1. It is also called the slope.
The bias (intercept): the output when the input is 0.

objects.text: w and b are parameters: numbers a model learns. In this course b always means the bias.

slides.notes:
The same function, written with letters, is the building block of machine learning. F of x equals w times x plus b. The letter w is the weight, how much the output grows for each extra unit of input. The letter b is the bias, also called the intercept, which is the output when the input is zero.

With w equal to two and b equal to one, and x equal to three, we get seven again. In machine learning, w and b are the parameters, the numbers a model learns from data. From today, the letter b in this course always means the bias, so whenever you see it, you know what it is.

title.text:
An exponential function multiplies
again and again, so it grows very fast

objects.alt: An exponential function multiplies again and again, so it grows very fast

objects.text: Exponential function: the input is the power. 2ˣ means x copies of 2 multiplied together: 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

runs.text: 2¹ = 2, 2² = 4, 2³ = 8: each step right doubles. Each step left halves, so 2⁰ = 1.
The base e ≈ 2.71828 gives eˣ: EXP(x), np.exp(x). eˣ is always above 0: e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37.

slides.notes:
An exponential function has the input up in the power. Two to the power x means x copies of two multiplied together, so two to the power three is two times two times two, which is eight. The values for one to five are two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two.

Each step to the right doubles the height. Walk the other way and each step halves, so two to the power zero is one. There is one special base in mathematics and machine learning, e, about two point seven one eight. In a spreadsheet you write EXP, and in Python np dot exp.

And e to any power is above zero, even for a negative power.

title.text:
A logarithm undoes an exponential: it
answers "which power gives this number?"

objects.alt: A logarithm undoes an exponential: it answers "which power gives this number?"

objects.text: The logarithm is the inverse of the exponential. If 2³ = 8, then log base 2 of 8 is 3.

runs.text: The curves eˣ and ln x are mirror images across the dashed line y = x.
ln x is the natural logarithm: the logarithm with base e.
ln 1 = 0, because e⁰ = 1. And ln x exists only for x above 0.

slides.notes:
A logarithm answers one question: which power gives this number?

Two to the power three is eight, so the logarithm base two of eight is three. In machine learning we almost always use the natural logarithm, written ln, which has base e. Look at the picture. The red curve is e to the x, and the black curve is ln of x.

They are mirror images across the dashed line, which is what inverse means. Look where ln of one sits: at zero. And ln only exists for numbers above zero. What do you think happens to ln x as x gets closer and closer to zero?

title.text:
The logarithm as a formula: the
answer x is the power that gives y

objects.alt: The logarithm as a formula: the answer x is the power that gives y

rows.text: The base: the number that is multiplied by itself. Common bases are 2, 10 and e ≈ 2.71828. (b stays the bias.)
The natural logarithm: the logarithm with base e.
The number we take the logarithm of. It must be above 0.
The answer: the power that a must be raised to, to give y.

objects.text: Python: np.log is natural, np.log10 is base 10. Spreadsheet: LN is natural, LOG10 is base 10.

slides.notes:
As a formula: the logarithm base a of y equals x exactly when a to the power x equals y. I call the base a, because b is kept for the bias. So log base two of eight is three, log base ten of a thousand is three, and ln of e is one.

The base is the number being multiplied. The number y must be above zero. And the answer x is the power. Watch the names in the tools. In Python, np dot log is the natural logarithm, and the base ten one is np dot log ten. In a spreadsheet, LN is natural and LOG10 is base ten.

title.text:
A probability lies between 0 and 1, so
its natural logarithm is zero or negative

objects.alt: A probability lies between 0 and 1, so its natural logarithm is zero or negative

objects.text: A certain event (p = 1) has ln p = 0. The smaller the probability, the more negative ln p.

runs.text: p = 1 gives 0. p = 0.5 gives −0.693.
Minus ln p grows as p shrinks.
For the right word it is the loss (the number training makes small).

slides.notes:
Logarithms and probabilities meet on this slide. A probability is between zero and one. Look at the curve of ln p on that range. At p equals one, the logarithm is zero. At one half it is minus zero point six nine three. At one tenth it is minus two point three, and at one in a hundred it is minus four point six.

The smaller the probability, the more negative the logarithm. If we flip the sign we get minus ln p, the negative log-probability, which is positive and grows as the event gets less likely. Training calls this number the loss, the score it tries to make small, and we see it at work near the end of today.

title.text:
Log rules: a logarithm turns
multiplying into adding

objects.alt: Log rules: a logarithm turns multiplying into adding

rows.text: Any number, used as a power.

objects.text: Check the quotient rule: ln(6 ÷ 2) = ln 3 = 1.0986, and ln 6 − ln 2 = 1.7918 − 0.6931 = 1.0986.

slides.notes:
Three log rules. The product rule says the log of u times v is the log of u plus the log of v. The quotient rule says the log of u divided by v is the log of u minus the log of v. And the power rule says the log of u to the power k is k times the log of u.

All three say one thing: a logarithm turns multiplying into adding. In the worked rows, ln six is one point seven nine one eight, the sum of ln two and ln three. And ln nine is twice ln three, two point one nine seven two, because nine is three squared.

If you know the log of ten, what is the log of a hundred?

title.text:
Check the product rule on the
curve: ln 2 plus ln 3 equals ln 6

objects.alt: Check the product rule on the curve: ln 2 plus ln 3 equals ln 6

objects.text: Product rule check with u = 2 and v = 3: ln 2 + ln 3 should equal ln 6.

runs.text: ln 2 = 0.6931 and ln 3 = 1.0986. Their sum is 1.7918.
The height of the curve at x = 6 is also 1.7918, because 2 × 3 = 6.
Heights on the curve add when the inputs multiply.

slides.notes:
We can check the product rule by hand. Read the heights from the curve. The natural log of two is zero point six nine three one. The natural log of three is one point zero nine eight six. Add them and you get one point seven nine one eight.

Now read the height of the curve at six, and it is one point seven nine one eight too, because two times three is six. The rule says heights on the curve add when the inputs multiply. This picture is the whole reason logarithms matter in AI: a long chain of multiplications becomes a chain of additions.

title.text:
A sentence has the probability of
all its words multiplied together

objects.alt: A sentence has the probability of all its words multiplied together

objects.text: Multiply the six word probabilities for the sentence. Add their logarithms for its log-probability.

slides.notes:
This is the sentence you will use in the lab, six words, with made-up probabilities. Each word has a probability that the model gave it, knowing the words before it. The sentence probability is all six multiplied: zero point three, times zero point two, times zero point five, times zero point four, times zero point seven, times zero point six two.

That is zero point zero zero five two zero eight. Now take the natural log of each word probability and add the six numbers. We get minus five point two five seven six, and the natural log of the product is the same number. Same answer, and now only additions, which is what you want for a thousand words.

title.text:
The log of a product is the sum of
the logs: ln P is the sum of the ln pᵢ

objects.alt: The log of a product is the sum of the logs: ln P is the sum of the ln pᵢ

rows.text: Multiply everything that comes after it. It is the product symbol.
The probability the model gave to word i, knowing the words before it.
The probability of the whole sentence.
The log-probability of the sentence: zero or negative.

objects.text: Plain average per word: 5.2576 ÷ 6 = 0.8763 nats, the training loss (cross-entropy, Session 17).

slides.notes:
The formula has a new symbol. A capital pi means multiply, the way a capital sigma means add. So P equals the product of all the word probabilities, p one times p two, and so on up to p n. The product rule, used again and again, says the log of P is the sum of the logs of the p values.

The right side has only additions. For our six words, the product is zero point zero zero five two zero eight, and the sum of the logs is minus five point two five seven six. Flip the sign and divide by six: the plain average per word is zero point eight seven six three.

That average over the words of a real text is the training loss of a language model, called cross-entropy, and its unit is nats because we used ln. Session seventeen returns to it.

title.text:
A long product of probabilities shrinks to zero,
but the sum of the logarithms stays usable

objects.alt: A long product of probabilities shrinks to zero, but the sum of the logarithms stays usable

objects.text: A computer stores numbers down to about 10⁻³⁰⁸. Below that, a product rounds to 0 (underflow).

slides.notes:
The practical reason is about storage. A computer stores numbers only down to about ten to the minus three hundred and eight. Below that it rounds to zero, which is called underflow. Take a text of one thousand words, where each word has probability zero point two. The product is about ten to the minus six hundred and ninety-nine, far below the limit, so the computer shows zero.

But the sum of the logarithms is one thousand times minus one point six one, which is minus one thousand six hundred and nine, an ordinary number. Real texts are long, so AI software always works with log-probabilities.

title.text: Common mistake: ln(u + v) differs from ln u + ln v

objects.text: Wrong

runs.text: ln(2 + 3) = ln 2 + ln 3
That gives 1.7918, but ln 5 is 1.6094.
np.log is base 10.

objects.text: Right

runs.text: np.log is the natural logarithm (base e).

objects.text: The log rules are for products only.

slides.notes:
This is the mistake I see most often. People read that a logarithm turns multiplying into adding, and then apply it to a sum. It does not. Take the natural log of two plus three. That is the log of five, which is one point six zero nine four.

The log of two plus the log of three is one point seven nine one eight, a different number. The rules are about products, quotients and powers only. The second trap is about tools. In Python, np dot log is the natural logarithm, and the base ten one has its own name.

Which of the two traps would catch you first?

title.text:
Read the recipe before you run it:
sums, logarithms and exponentials

runs.text: total = np.sum(p)
neg_log_p = -np.log(p)
entropy = np.sum(p * neg_log_p)
sentence_p = np.prod(word_p)
back = np.exp(np.log(6))

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1: the five probabilities in a list called an array.
Line 2: add them up, which is the sigma sum.
Line 3: minus ln of each one, all at once.
Line 4: each p times its minus ln p, added up: the entropy, 1.133 nats (Session 17). Spreadsheet: SUMPRODUCT.
Line 5: multiply all six word probabilities. Spreadsheet: =PRODUCT(B27:B32).
Line 6: EXP undoes LN, so you get 6 back.

slides.notes:
Read the recipe before the lab. In Python, np dot array makes a list of numbers we can compute with. Np dot sum is the sigma sum. Minus np dot log of p takes minus ln of every probability at once. Line four multiplies each probability by its own minus ln and adds the results.

That number has a name, the entropy, one point one three three nats, and Session seventeen explains it. In a spreadsheet it is SUMPRODUCT. Line five multiplies a whole list, np dot prod in Python and PRODUCT in a spreadsheet. The last line shows that EXP and LN undo each other.

title.text:
Four messages you may meet,
what they mean and what to do

rows.text: nan or a RuntimeWarning from np.log, or #NUM! from LN
You took the log of 0 or of a negative number. A logarithm needs a number above 0.
Check the probabilities. None may be 0 or negative.
That is correct. A probability below 1 has a negative natural logarithm.
Use minus ln p when you want a positive number.
Underflow: the true value is about 10⁻⁶⁹⁹, too small to store.
Use the sum of the logs. That is the point of the step.
The function name is misspelt, or your region uses a semicolon between the arguments.
Retype the function. Try ; instead of ,

slides.notes:
Four messages you may meet. A nan, a warning, or the error hash NUM means you took the log of zero or of a negative number, so check the probabilities. A negative log-probability is correct, because a probability below one has a negative natural log. A product that shows zero is underflow, which is exactly what step seven is about.

And hash NAME in a spreadsheet usually means a misspelt function, or a region that wants a semicolon. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: a probability
for every possible next word

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: a probability for every possible next word

objects.text: Language models of this kind give every possible next token a probability.

runs.text: A token is a piece of text, often a word or part of a word.
These numbers are illustrative (made up). They add up to 1.
Vocabulary of open models: Llama 2, 32,000 tokens; Gemma, 256,000.

slides.notes:
ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and other assistants are products built on large language models. Their exact designs are not published, but published research describes how models of this kind work. They read the text so far and give every possible next token a probability. A token is a piece of text, often a word or part of a word.

Here are five candidate tokens with made-up probabilities that add up to one. Open models publish their vocabulary size: Llama 2 has thirty-two thousand tokens and Gemma about two hundred and fifty-six thousand, and the model scores all of them at every step. Which token would the model most likely choose here?

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: training
uses ln of the right word probability

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: training uses ln of the right word probability

objects.text: Training scores the model by minus ln p, where p is the probability it gave the word that really came next.

runs.text: The right word is Kampala. With p = 0.62 the loss is 0.478.
With only p = 0.04 the loss is 3.219. A low probability on the right word gives a high loss.
Averaged over a text: cross-entropy (Session 17).

slides.notes:
This graph is the link to training. Published research describes language models of this kind as trained to predict the next token. For each position in a text, the model gives a probability to the token that really came next. The training score for that position is minus ln of that probability, called the loss.

If the model gave Kampala zero point six two, the loss is zero point four seven eight. If it gave only zero point zero four, the loss is three point two one nine. So a low probability on the right word means a high loss, and training pushes the loss down.

Averaged over every word of a text, as you did for the six-word sentence, it is called the cross-entropy loss, and we meet it properly in Session seventeen.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: What is Σ pᵢ for i = 1 to 3, when p₁ = 0.5, p₂ = 0.3 and p₃ = 0.2?
Fill the gap: ln 12 = ln 3 + ln ?
ln 4, because 3 × 4 = 12 and the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.
Why do AI programs add log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?
A product of many small probabilities underflows to 0. A sum of logs stays an ordinary number.

slides.notes:
Last, the exit check. Three questions. Write your answers in your notes before you look at mine. One, with p one equal to point five, p two point three and p three point two, what is the sigma sum?

Two, fill the gap: ln twelve equals ln three plus ln what?

Three, why do AI programs add log-probabilities and not multiply probabilities?

The short answers are on the slide. If you got all three, you are ready for vectors next session. If one surprised you, look at that part of the lab again tonight.
